extracted.intended_audience: Reuters reporters, editors and newsroom staff (wire journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Operational and style rules for filing, formatting and updating breaking-news stories, alerts, newsbreaks, updates, wrapups, skedlines and related newsroom processes on the Reuters wire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single/Multi-take filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are to be filed in a single take (page) in nearly all circumstances; a second take is used only occasionally, most commonly to add cross-reference information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a second take is necessary it must use the same Unique Story Number (USN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct injection / self-publishing restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Designated staff may publish Alerts; reporters must not publish directly to clients without a 'second pair of eyes', preferably a senior reporter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regional desk retains overall responsibility for quality of any self-published or directly injected items; publishing rights may be removed from reporters who abuse them. Anything beyond a Brief or Urgent must be filed by an editing desk. Corrections to directly injected items should be handled by the regional desk. Arrangements for self publishing/direct injection must be agreed with the relevant filing desk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-submission checks for stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sending copy to an editing desk, reporters should re-read the story and perform simple checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks include: re-read story and lead to ensure important information and context are at top; check RICs; check for typos and grammatical errors; ensure adequate sourcing, accuracy and fairness. These checks help the desk handle the story quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a second pair of eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask a colleague in your bureau to read the story carefully before sending it to a desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The colleague must be critical and ensure the story is adequately sourced, accurate, fair and concise. Most errors can be caught in the bureau.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve senior staff on problem stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Problematic stories should be copyedited by a senior reporter, bureau charge or editor in charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring in the bureau chief or an editor in charge for stories with editorial or sourcing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing to an editing desk via Lynx Editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters file to a regional editing desk by using the TRANSFER button in Lynx Editor and choosing the appropriate desk basket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a TRANSFER keyboard shortcut (Ctrl+T to send to default, Alt+T to open dropdown). In Lynx Editor the Alerting Tool is accessed under the New button. Use TASTE or EDIT baskets as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not open stories in edit mode in desk taste baskets / requesting returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if permissioned for access to desk TASTE or EDIT baskets, reporters should not open a story in edit mode in an editing desk taste basket as it prevents editors from handling the story in a timely way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reporter needs a story returned, screentop or phone the desk and ask for it to be sent back to the reporter's reporting team or bureau edit basket. Stories cannot be returned to a reporter's personal basket because only one live version exists at any time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk hours and contact methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must be aware of desk hours of operation and key telephone numbers; desk staff should know hours and contacts in other regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fastest contact method is the screentop messaging system in Lynx Editor; email is also acceptable. Make sure you are available to handle queries and leave a contact phone number if you must step away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black hole filing methods (emergency/offline filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two methods for filing when normal systems unavailable: 1) web-based filing to file.reuters.com; 2) email to file@reuters.com using coded subject line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method 1: write story offline, log into website, fill in address codes, slug, headline, paste story, transmit. Note: cannot file to wire, only to taste/service baskets. Method 2: write in personal email, subject must be address codes and slug in all caps with spaces in precise places (e.g. YLP # BC-SLUG) and send to file@reuters.com. Common errors: omitting spaces between codes, hash sign and slug, or not using all caps. In poor comms, write offline and paste into email compose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alert format and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alert (also snap or bulletin) is the highest priority item for Reuters services and has strict format and style rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Alert should be up to 100 characters (some products cannot handle longer); written entirely in upper case (except lower-case letters in RICs); sourced (rare exceptions: routine corporate results or scheduled indicators); written in present tense; filed at priority 1; normally filed without a dateline (dateline allowed only if location needed for clarity, used only in first in series and separated by ' - '). Use simple everyday nouns, active present tense verbs, avoid slang and jargon, and use known abbreviations. File Alerts when news may move a market or influence client decisions or be of significant interest to a global readership. Avoid flooding with more than ~5 alerts on a single newsbreak.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to file an Alert
rubrics_metrics.description: File an Alert when you judge that news may move a market, influence client decisions, or be of significant interest to a global readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of an Alert as a long headline with a source that tells the reader the essential facts only. Don't cheapen its value by using Alerts when not justified; clarity and precise sourcing are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsbreak (Urgent) format and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Newsbreak (urgent/rush) usually follows an Alert and is filed at Priority 2; it puts facts into context and should follow quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsbreaks must use the same USN as the Alert(s). The slugline must include the word URGENT in brackets. Most Newsbreaks should be no more than two paragraphs or 100 words (about 10 lines) for unexpected news. Aim to have a Newsbreak on the wire within 5–15 minutes of an Alert; desks will chase if not covered within 15 minutes. If unlikely to move a market but requires a quick start, start with a Newsbreak followed within 30 minutes by an Update 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsbreak content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A Newsbreak must contain the main facts, the source, circumstances and the time element, and should answer the 'So what?' question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It must put the news in context, signal significance, give comparisons, and include market reaction if immediately available. An authoritative quote is desirable but don't delay the Newsbreak for a quote. For predictable events, prepare background and pre-written quotes to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update definition, tagging and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: An Update carries forward an earlier report by weaving in fresh developments, reaction, added context, interpretation, analysis and background. Use UPDATE tags in sluglines and headlines (UPDATE 1, UPDATE 2, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a new Unique Story Number for the Update and retain it throughout the Update series. UPDATEs should always contain the latest available information and analysis, but the latest information isn't always the most important — twin it with the key point from earlier stories or leave the lead unchanged and add fresh information lower down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update length and timing guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Length and timing norms for Updates to ensure speed and usability for clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UPDATE 1s to Newsbreaks should be no more than about 200 words (20 lines) or about five paragraphs, and filed within 30 minutes of the Newsbreak. Most breaking news updates, sidebars and intra-day market reports should be no more than about 500 words (50 lines). The final update or wrapup may run to about 800 words (80 lines). Desks should fix and move problematic early updates quickly, trimming overwritten copy to move update1s and update2s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequent updates and retention rules
rubrics_metrics.description: How subsequent updates should behave in a series and how to retain earlier material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsequent UPDATES replace the previous Update in the series. Fresh UPDATES should retain most of the factual material in earlier stories to avoid loss of content and to enable corrections. Include an ADVISORY LINE under the headline telling readers what has been updated (e.g., 'Adds king's quotes in third paragraph'). An update series usually restarts at midnight local time with a spot story and UPDATE 1 but use common sense for near-midnight events. Stories can be updated as much as 36 hours after first transmission if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrapup purpose and format
rubrics_metrics.description: A WRAPUP is a synthesis providing a broad snapshot of latest developments in a top story — more than the last Update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Wrapup should pull together news from more than one dateline or series; carry the dateline/byline of the writer with the strongest story; lead on the hardest news and weave significant developments high up (top ~35 lines); be no more than 800 words (~80 lines); be freshened as new developments occur; bring in essential background, analysis, color and context and remove material no longer required. Wrapups should not include secondary material that is not essential and should not be freshened unless there are new developments or the story can be refined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lynx NewsPlanner and skedline requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All bureau chiefs and EICs must ensure their reporting teams update Lynx NewsPlanner calendars and file skedlines for expected/top-news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NewsPlanner entries should include expected headline and a sentence or two explaining what the story will be about and its significance, likely slug, reporter, filing time and estimated word count. Skedline format: HEADLINE: DATELINE: LEAD: Main elements of story with context on its significance. Include slug and expected tags (e.g., UPDATE X, PIX, VIDEO). Use GMT (add local time for AMERS), 24-hour clock with no colon (e.g., 1430). Transfer skedline to GLOBAL-SCHEDULES basket in Lynx Editor. Send skedlines at least 30 minutes before the schedule is published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media schedule times and publishing windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard media schedule times that desks publish Business and World News schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business Schedule (London/New York/Singapore): GMT 0230, 0630, 0830, 1230, 1430, 1830 in European summer; alternate winter schedule provided for EST. World News schedule times listed for summer and winter (e.g., GMT 0200, 0600, 1000, 1400, 1800, 2200 in summer). Watch clock-change weeks; use timeanddate.com/worldclock for checks. Other schedules exist for Sports, Entertainment, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: The breaking-news drill: practical tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational advice to make the Alert/Newsbreak/Update drill work efficiently on major stories and scheduled events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-write background and context where possible; double-staff key events and hand off writing of Alerts/Newsbreaks; desks can cut overwritten updates to move faster; avoid proliferating separate update series — most stories need a single trunk; consult the desk and send skedlines; work from edited copy when updating to avoid re-editing; add 'trashlines' or advisory lines noting what was added/changed in each update; boldface changes to help editors (desks should remove bold before publishing); don't 'file and flee' — leave contact phone number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid inventing acronyms/abbreviations; use abbreviations only when they don't impede clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reader should not have to read backwards to understand an abbreviation. Use a generic term rather than stuffing a story with initials. Well-known abbreviations (e.g., AIDS, NATO) may be used alone at first reference with full name subsequently. Abbreviations of two initials take full stops (U.S., U.N.) except EU and UK; full stops may be omitted in alerts/headlines for space. Abbreviations of three or more initials and acronyms do not take full stops (IBM, UNICEF). Form plural of abbreviations by adding a lower-case s (ICBMs). Do not use full stops when abbreviating months in datelines (Jan, Feb, etc.); in text abbreviate months when used with a specific date (Jan. 19, Dec. 25).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acronyms guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid acronyms where possible because few are understandable at first reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace acronyms with a noun like 'the committee' or 'the organisation' where possible. If initials are well known (e.g., PLO) you need not bracket them after first reference; if little known bracket initials after first reference (e.g., Western European Union (WEU)). Do not bracket initials if you're not going to use them again lower in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives and hyphenation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use adjectives sparingly and prefer strong verbs and facts; follow hyphenation rules for adjectival phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more than two adjectives precede a single noun, rewrite the sentence. Avoid adjectives that imply judgment. Hyphenate adjective+noun pairs used adjectivally (blue-chip share). Hyphenate adjective + past participle when used adjectivally (old-fashioned morality). Do not hyphenate an adverb and adjective when they stand alone (well known artist), but hyphenate if they are paired to form a single adjective (well-known artist). Do not hyphenate when the adverb ends in -ly (poorly planned operation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic titles capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize academic titles only when they immediately precede a personal name; otherwise use lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Professor John Smith (capitalised before name) vs the professor (lower case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific word-usage rules (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on preferred word choices and common misspellings to maintain clarity and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the guide: 'access' should not be used as a verb; use 'accidentally' not 'accidently'; use 'accolade' not 'acolade'; use 'accommodate' not 'accomodate'; 'achilles’ heel' uses apostrophe and capitalisation; prefer 'acknowledgment' rather than 'acknowledgement'. Convert acres to hectares guidance provided (multiply by 0.405). Use American/other regional variants where noted (e.g., 'ageing' vs American 'aging').
